entries.title: Eggs to order and the omelette
entries.say: As it reads: eggs to order and the omelette.
entries.summary: Fried, scrambled, boiled and rolled: the everyday eggs of a breakfast kitchen, each a matter of heat, fat and timing. The cook makes exactly what the ticket asks, and the French omelette is the test every cook is set.
entries.guest: How do you like your egg? I will write it exactly: over easy, sunny side up or scrambled. Our Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn.

paras: Eggs to order are the short list a breakfast cook makes all morning: fried, scrambled, boiled and the omelette. Each is the same egg given a different heat, fat and time, so a cook learns them by name and a server writes them word for word.

Two facts sit under all of them. Egg white begins to set at about 62°C (144°F); the yolk thickens at about 65°C (149°F) and sets by about 70°C (158°F), so a few degrees decide whether it runs, turns jammy or sets. And eggs keep cooking off the heat, so the cook stops early and lets carryover finish.

Fried eggs: crack each egg into a small dish first, to keep the yolk whole, then slide it into butter foaming over a medium-low flame. Sunny side up is never turned, its yolk left runny. Basted means a lid on the pan, or spoonfuls of hot butter, so a thin veil of white sets over the yolk. Turned eggs are flipped gently: over easy for 20 to 30 seconds, the yolk runny; over medium for about a minute, the yolk jammy; over hard until the yolk is set.

Scrambled eggs come two ways. The French way, oeufs brouillés, is eggs beaten with salt and stirred without stopping in butter over low heat until they thicken into small, creamy curds, with cold butter or cream stirred in to stop the cooking. The American way is quicker, over medium heat, with larger, firmer curds. Either way they leave the heat while still slightly wet, because carryover finishes them on the plate.

Boiled eggs are lowered from the fridge into water at a steady simmer, so the timing is exact and they peel more easily; a simmer, not a hard boil, keeps them from cracking. For a large egg, about 6 minutes gives a set white and a runny yolk, a minute or two more a jammy one, and 10 to 11 minutes a set yolk. Then into iced water, which stops the cooking, eases peeling and prevents the grey-green ring that forms when sulphur from an overcooked white meets the iron in the yolk.

The French omelette is the cook's test. Beat 3 eggs with a pinch of salt until no streaks of white remain. Heat 15 g (1 tbsp) of butter in a 20 cm (8 inch) pan over brisk heat until it foams, never browns, then pour in the eggs and stir fast with a fork while shaking the pan, so they set in small, soft curds. After about 30 seconds, while the top is still moist, baveuse in French, roll it away from the handle and turn it out seam down: pale, smooth and soft at the centre.
3 eggs and 15 g (1 tbsp) of butter in a 20 cm (8 inch) pan for a French omelette; about 6 minutes for a soft-boiled large egg, 10 to 11 for hard; 20 to 30 seconds on the second side for over easy.

The American omelette is set flat, not stirred: the cook lifts the edges so raw egg runs under, lays the filling over one half, folds it and slides it out, firmer and lightly golden. The filling goes in warm, cooked and drained, because a cold one holds the eggs on the heat. Both need an egg pan, kept for eggs alone, never scoured and sized to the eggs, so they set neither thin and rubbery nor thick and raw.

Most egg faults are heat faults: lacy brown edges, rubbery whites, a watery scramble, a browned omelette. A broken yolk comes from cracking straight into the pan or flipping roughly; a grey ring from too long in the pot or no iced water after.

Brennan's breakfast carries a soft-boiled egg on the Eggs Owen, its yolk running into the short rib débris, and a sunny-side-up egg on the Duck Confit Waffle and, from Vital Farms, on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. The Crab & Corn Omelette holds Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Egg Any Style is one egg, made as the ticket reads.

Ask the style and the doneness and write them exactly. Describe the omelette by its filling until lineup says whether it is rolled or folded, and which styles the kitchen offers. A firmer egg on a signature plate, or a question about runny yolks, means a check with the kitchen, not a promise.

faults.fault: Brown, lacy edges on a fried egg
faults.cause: The pan or the fat was too hot.
faults.fix: Fry over medium-low heat in butter that foams but does not colour.

faults.cause: Overcooked: the curds tightened and squeezed out their water.
faults.fix: Cook lower and slower, and take them off the heat while they still look slightly wet.

faults.cause: The butter browned before the eggs went in, or the eggs stayed too long on the heat.
faults.fix: Pour the eggs in as the butter foams, stir to small curds and roll while the centre is soft.

faults.fault: Grey-green ring round a boiled yolk
faults.cause: Cooked too long, or left to cool slowly in its own heat.
faults.fix: Time the eggs from the moment they go in, then plunge them straight into iced water.

faults.cause: A cold or wet filling kept the eggs on the heat.
faults.fix: Add the filling warm, already cooked and drained.

brennans.how: Filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Ask at lineup whether the kitchen rolls it French style or folds it, so you can describe it before it lands.

A soft-boiled egg comes with the red wine braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, so the yolk runs into everything. Soft-boiled classically means about six minutes in the shell; confirm the kitchen's timing at lineup.
A sunny-side-up egg from Vital Farms, pasture-raised, sits beside the steak and the smoked potato pavé, its runny yolk meeting the béarnaise. The menu names Vital Farms on this plate.
One egg, cooked as the guest asks: the style and the doneness written on the ticket are the whole recipe, so write them exactly, and confirm at lineup which styles the kitchen offers.
A sunny-side-up egg tops the crisp duck confit leg on the cornbread and chive waffle; a guest who wants it cooked another way is a question for the kitchen before any promise.

cards.front: What is a sunny-side-up egg?
cards.back: A fried egg that is never turned: the white set, the yolk runny and bright on top. A lid or spoonfuls of hot butter can veil it, which makes it basted.

cards.front: How do over easy, over medium and over hard differ?
cards.back: All three are fried and turned. Over easy keeps the yolk runny, over medium leaves it jammy, over hard cooks it right through: different eggs, so the ticket names the style exactly.

cards.front: Why do scrambled eggs come off the heat before they look done?
cards.back: Carryover: the heat already in the eggs keeps cooking them on the warm plate, so eggs that look done in the pan arrive overcooked.

cards.front: How are scrambled eggs made the French way?
cards.back: Beaten with salt and stirred without stopping in butter over low heat into small, creamy curds, then finished with cold butter or cream to stop the cooking.

cards.front: How long does a large egg need, lowered into simmering water?
cards.back: About 6 minutes for a set white and a runny yolk, a minute or two more for jammy, and 10 to 11 minutes for a set yolk.

cards.front: Why do boiled eggs go straight into iced water?
cards.back: It stops the cooking, makes them easier to peel and prevents the grey-green ring that forms round an overcooked yolk.

cards.front: What does baveuse mean for a French omelette?
cards.back: Still moist and creamy at the centre when it is rolled: the omelette is pale and unbrowned outside and soft within.

cards.front: What goes into a classic French omelette, and in what pan?
cards.back: 3 eggs beaten smooth with salt and 15 g (1 tbsp) of butter, in a 20 cm (8 inch) egg pan over brisk heat.

cards.front: Why does the filling of a folded omelette go in warm?
cards.back: A cold filling keeps the eggs on the heat while it warms through, so they overcook; a warm, drained filling lets them finish soft.

cards.front: What makes a good egg pan?
cards.back: Kept for eggs alone, seasoned or non-stick and never scoured, and sized to the eggs, so they set neither thin and rubbery nor thick and raw.

cards.front: How hot should the butter be when the omelette eggs go in?
cards.back: Foaming but never brown: the foam shows the pan is hot enough, and browned butter would colour and flavour a French omelette wrongly.

cards.front: Which eggs do Brennan's breakfast plates carry?
cards.back: A soft-boiled egg on the Eggs Owen, a sunny-side-up egg on the hanger steak and the Duck Confit Waffle, the Crab & Corn Omelette and Egg Any Style.

questions.q: A ticket reads over medium. How should the yolk arrive?
questions.answer: Jammy, partly set
distractors: Runny, the egg never turned
Set hard right through
Scrambled into the white
questions.why: Over medium is turned and cooked about a minute on the second side, so the yolk thickens to jam; over easy stays runny and over hard sets.

questions.q: Why does a cook take scrambled eggs off the heat while they still look wet?
questions.answer: Carryover heat finishes them on the plate
distractors: Wet eggs hold their colour longer on the pass
The salt needs time to dissolve
Wet eggs reheat better if they wait
questions.why: The heat already in the eggs keeps cooking them after the pan, so eggs that look done in the pan reach the guest dry and weeping.

questions.q: Roughly how long does a large egg need in simmering water for a set white and a runny yolk?
questions.answer: About 6 minutes
distractors: About 2 minutes
About 12 minutes
About 20 minutes
questions.why: Six minutes sets the white while the yolk stays liquid; 10 to 11 minutes sets the yolk, and much longer brings the grey ring.

questions.q: What does plunging boiled eggs into iced water prevent?
questions.answer: A grey-green ring round the yolk
distractors: A runny white
Salt soaking through the shell
The shell cracking in the pot
questions.why: Iced water stops the cooking; left hot, sulphur from the white meets iron in the yolk and leaves a grey-green ring.

questions.q: What does a French cook mean by an omelette baveuse?
questions.answer: Soft and creamy at the centre
distractors: Browned and crisp on the outside
Folded around a filling
Cooked through and firm
questions.why: A French omelette is rolled while its centre is still moist and creamy, and it stays pale outside; firm and golden is the American style.

questions.q: Why is the filling of an American omelette added warm?
questions.answer: So the eggs do not overcook
distractors: So the cheese turns brown
So the omelette folds more easily
So the filling melts into the eggs
questions.why: A cold filling chills the eggs and keeps them on the heat while it warms through, so the omelette turns firm and dry.

questions.q: When should the beaten eggs go into the omelette pan?
questions.answer: When the butter foams, before it browns
distractors: When the butter has turned nut-brown
Before the butter has melted
When the butter starts to smoke
questions.why: Foaming butter shows the pan is hot enough to set the eggs fast; browned butter colours and flavours a French omelette, which should be pale.

questions.q: What makes a fried egg sunny side up?
questions.answer: It is never turned
distractors: It is turned once, briefly
Its yolk is cooked until firm
It is finished under the salamander
questions.why: Sunny side up cooks on one side only, the white set and the yolk runny on top; any turned egg is over easy, medium or hard.

questions.q: Which egg does the Eggs Owen carry at Brennan's?
questions.answer: A soft-boiled egg
distractors: A poached egg
A sunny-side-up egg
Scrambled eggs
questions.why: The Eggs Owen tops its red wine braised short rib débris with a soft-boiled egg, so the yolk runs into the meat and the sauces.

questions.q: A ticket for Egg Any Style just says fried. What must the server add before it goes to the kitchen?
questions.answer: The style and doneness, such as over medium
distractors: Nothing: the cook chooses the style
Only how many eggs the guest wants on the plate
Whether the guest wants toast with it
questions.why: The ticket is the whole recipe for an egg cooked to order: over easy and over medium are different eggs, so the server writes the style exactly.

entries.title: Boil, blanch and steam
entries.say: As it reads: boil, blanch and steam.
entries.summary: Three water methods every cook uses daily: a rolling boil in salted water for pasta and green vegetables, a brief blanch and an iced refresh to set colour and prepare for service, and steam for gentle, moist cooking that keeps shape.
entries.guest: Blanched means cooked briefly in boiling water and cooled fast, which keeps vegetables bright and crisp; steamed means cooked over the water, never in it, so the food stays moist.

paras: Boiling, blanching and steaming are the plainest ways heat meets food: through water, or the steam rising from it. Water at a full boil, 100°C (212°F) at sea level, gets no hotter however hard the flame, so nothing browns and the food tastes of itself. The skill is in the details: how much water and salt, how long, and what happens when the food comes out.

Boiling cooks food through in the water. Blanching, blanchir in French, uses the same boiling water for a brief plunge only. Steaming holds the food above the water, in its vapour. The gentler poach and the simmer have their own entry.

Boiling means a full rolling boil: big bubbles that keep breaking even when the food goes in and the pot is stirred. Use plenty of water, about 1 litre (about 1 quart) for every 100 g (3.5 oz) of pasta or vegetables, so it comes back to the boil quickly, and salt it well, about 10 g to the litre, so the food is seasoned all through. Green vegetables boiled this way and served plainly with butter are called à l'anglaise, in the English style.

Blanching is a brief plunge in boiling water: seconds for spinach and herbs, 2 to 3 minutes for green beans. It sets the colour of green vegetables, loosens skins, tames bitterness and part-cooks food to be finished in moments during service. Refreshing, rafraîchir, follows at once: into iced water to stop the cooking and hold the green, only until cold, then drained and dried well, because clinging water thins the butter or sauce it meets later.

Monder is blanching to peel. Score a small cross in the base of a tomato, plunge it into boiling water for 10 to 15 seconds, until the skin curls at the cross, then refresh it and slip the skin off; peeled, seeded and diced, it becomes a concassée. Peaches are skinned the same way after about 20 to 30 seconds, and almonds after about a minute, when the skins slip off between the fingers. Bones and meat for a white stock are blanched from cold: brought up to the boil, boiled a few minutes, then drained and rinsed of their grey scum, so the stock starts clear.

Steaming cooks food in the vapour above boiling water: a basket or perforated tray over a pan with a close lid, the food never touching the water. Steam gives up a great deal of heat as it condenses on the food, so steaming is quick yet gentle, and fish, vegetables and dumplings keep their shape and flavour instead of losing them to the water. A combi oven, combining steam with fan heat, steams whole trays at once; a parcel of leaf or paper, the method of en papillote, steams food in its own juices.

Green vegetables turn olive and dull when cooked too long, covered, or with acid. Heat releases acids from the vegetable's own cells, and acid turns bright green chlorophyll into an olive-brown pigment. A large pot of fast-boiling water cooks them quickly, and an open pot lets some of those acids escape in the steam, so cook them fast and uncovered, and add lemon or vinegar only at the end. Bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) keeps the green but turns vegetables mushy and soapy, so the classical kitchen relies on speed.

Creamed spinach, under the Eggs Sardou and as a breakfast and lunch side, is classically spinach blanched, plunged into iced water and squeezed hard before the cream goes in, so it stays rich rather than watery; how the kitchen builds ours, and whether the two are one preparation, are questions for the kitchen. Buttered noodles, on the children's dinner, are classically pasta boiled in well-salted water until just tender, then tossed with butter and grated cheese; the menu names neither the shape nor the cheese, so the kitchen has the answer.

Steam burns harder than boiling water, because it gives up its heat as it condenses on skin. Tilt a lid away from you as you lift it, stand back as a combi oven door opens, and lower food into boiling water rather than dropping it.

These words reach the dining room on menus and in questions. Blanched means briefly boiled and cooled; steamed, cooked over water, never in it; à l'anglaise, plainly boiled and buttered. A request for vegetables steamed rather than buttered goes to the kitchen, not a promise.

ratios.label: Water for pasta and vegetables
ratios.value: About 1 litre (about 1 quart) for every 100 g (3.5 oz)

ratios.label: Tomatoes to peel by monder
ratios.value: 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water

faults.cause: Cooked too long, covered, in too little water, or with acid added early.
faults.fix: Boil fast in plenty of water, uncovered, refresh in iced water and add acid only at the last moment.

faults.cause: Left in the iced water too long, or not drained and dried.
faults.fix: Refresh only until cold, then drain well and dry on a cloth.

faults.cause: The water was under-salted or barely boiling.
faults.fix: Salt the water to about 10 g a litre and keep it at a rolling boil.

faults.fault: Tomato flesh soft under the peel
faults.cause: Left in the boiling water too long.
faults.fix: Give it 10 to 15 seconds, until the skin curls at the cross, then straight into iced water.

faults.cause: The bones were not blanched and rinsed of their scum first.
faults.fix: Start the bones in cold water, boil briefly, then drain and rinse before the stock begins.

faults.cause: The water touched the food, or drips fell from the lid.
faults.fix: Keep the water well below the basket and lift the lid away so drips fall back into the pan.

brennans.how: Creamed spinach is classically blanched, plunged into iced water and squeezed hard before the cream goes in. How the kitchen builds this side, and whether it matches the Sardou's spinach, is confirmed at lineup.

cards.front: What is a rolling boil?
cards.back: Big bubbles that keep breaking even when food goes in and the pot is stirred: water at 100°C (212°F) at sea level, as hot as it gets.

cards.front: How much salt goes in the water for pasta and green vegetables?
cards.back: About 10 g to 1 litre (about 1 quart), so the food is seasoned all through as it cooks.

cards.front: What does à l'anglaise mean for vegetables?
cards.back: In the English style: boiled in plenty of salted water and served plainly, usually with butter.

cards.front: What is blanching, and why do it?
cards.back: A brief plunge in boiling water: it sets green colour, loosens skins, tames bitterness or part-cooks food so it finishes fast in service.

cards.front: What is refreshing, rafraîchir, in the kitchen?
cards.back: Plunging blanched food straight into iced water to stop the cooking and hold the colour, then draining and drying it well.

cards.front: How is a tomato peeled by monder?
cards.back: Score a cross in the base, boil it for 10 to 15 seconds until the skin curls, refresh it in iced water, then slip the skin off.

cards.front: Why do green vegetables turn olive?
cards.back: Acid, from the vegetable's own cells or added, turns bright chlorophyll olive-brown, and long, covered cooking gives it time to act.

cards.front: How do you keep green vegetables bright?
cards.back: Cook them fast in a large pot of fast-boiling water, uncovered so some of their acids escape in the steam, then refresh them in iced water and add acid only at the end.

cards.front: Why does steaming keep food moist and in shape?
cards.back: The food sits above the water, so little leaches out and nothing jostles it, while condensing steam gives up its heat quickly.

cards.front: How are bones blanched for a white stock?
cards.back: Covered with cold water, brought to the boil, boiled briefly, then drained and rinsed of scum, so the stock starts clear.

cards.front: What is a combi oven?
cards.back: An oven that combines steam with fan heat, so a kitchen can steam whole trays at once or roast with moisture.

cards.front: Why not add bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) to keep beans green?
cards.back: It holds the colour but turns vegetables mushy with a soapy taste, so the classical kitchen relies on speed instead.

questions.q: Which is a good reason to blanch a vegetable?
questions.answer: To set its colour and part-cook it for service
distractors: To brown its surface for flavour
To cook it slowly until it is soft enough to purée
To preserve it for months under fat
questions.why: A brief plunge in boiling water sets the green, loosens skins and part-cooks food, so it can be finished in moments during service.

questions.q: What happens straight after green beans are blanched for service?
questions.answer: They go into iced water, then are drained
distractors: They rest covered in the hot pot
They are tossed in lemon juice
They cool slowly in their own cooking water
questions.why: Refreshing in iced water stops the cooking and holds the green; draining and drying stop water thinning the butter or sauce later.

questions.q: What turns long-cooked green beans olive?
questions.answer: Acid acting on the chlorophyll
distractors: Too much salt in the boiling water
Cooling them in iced water
Too much water in the pot
questions.why: Heat releases acids from the plant's own cells, and acid turns bright chlorophyll olive-brown; long, covered cooking gives it time to work.

questions.q: Why are green vegetables boiled uncovered in a large pot?
questions.answer: They cook fast and acids escape in the steam
distractors: Uncovered water boils at a higher temperature
A large pot keeps the beans from sticking together
A lid would make the beans steam rather than boil
questions.why: Plenty of water returns to the boil quickly and an open pot lets some volatile acids escape, so the vegetables cook before they dull.

questions.q: How long does a ripe tomato need in boiling water to slip its skin?
questions.answer: About 10 to 15 seconds
distractors: About 1 to 2 minutes
About 3 to 4 minutes
About 45 to 60 seconds
questions.why: Seconds are enough for the skin to curl back at the scored cross; any longer and the flesh beneath starts to cook and soften.

questions.q: Roughly how much salt seasons boiling water for pasta?
questions.answer: About 10 g to 1 litre (about 1 quart)
distractors: A pinch for the whole pot
About 100 g to 1 litre (about 1 quart)
None, since salt toughens pasta
questions.why: Around 10 g a litre seasons pasta and vegetables all through as they cook; a pinch does nothing, and ten times that is a brine.

questions.q: Why are bones for a white stock started in cold water and boiled briefly first?
questions.answer: To draw out scum so the stock stays clear
distractors: To brown them for a darker stock
To dissolve all their gelatine quickly
To season them before roasting
questions.why: Starting cold and boiling briefly draws impurities out as grey scum; draining and rinsing take it away, so the white stock starts clear.

questions.q: What keeps steamed fish moist and whole?
questions.answer: It cooks above the water, never in it
distractors: It cooks in fat below a simmer
It is turned often in a hot pan
It is boiled hard in well-salted water
questions.why: Held above the water in the vapour, the fish is neither jostled nor leached, while condensing steam cooks it quickly and gently.

entries.title: En papillote
entries.summary: Food sealed in a parcel of paper, foil or leaf and baked, so it steams in its own juices with its aromatics. The parcel puffs as the steam builds, and the burst of scent when it is opened is the point.
entries.guest: En papillote means in paper: the fish is sealed in a parcel and baked, so it steams in its own juices. Ours is wrapped in banana leaf, with tomato, olives and crab.

paras: En papillote, said ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means in paper. The food, most often fish, is sealed in a parcel with aromatics, butter or oil and a splash of liquid, then baked. Inside, the liquid and the fish's own juices turn to steam, so the food cooks gently and moistly, and every bit of aroma stays trapped until the parcel is cut open. It is steaming in a closed package, done in the oven.

It suits delicate fillets of white fish and salmon, scallops, chicken breast and young vegetables: foods that cook quickly and would dry out under fiercer heat. Because nothing escapes, the juices left in the parcel become the sauce.

Cut a large heart of baking parchment, about 30 to 35 cm (12 to 14 inches) across, and brush it with butter or oil. On one half lay a bed of aromatics cut fine enough to cook in the time the fish takes: a julienne, thin matchsticks, of leek, carrot and fennel, with sliced shallot, herbs and lemon. Set the seasoned fillet on top, add a knob of butter or a spoon of oil and 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) of white wine or stock. Fold the paper over, then crimp the edges in small, tight, overlapping folds all the way round and twist the tip, so no steam can escape.

Bake the parcels on a tray in a hot oven, about 200°C (392°F). Time by thickness: a fillet 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick needs roughly 12 to 15 minutes, a thinner one less. The parcel puffs as the steam builds, which shows the inside is at full steam. Fish is done when it flakes and reaches 63°C (145°F) at its thickest point, which a probe through the paper of a test parcel can confirm. Serve at once, before the parcel sags.

The wrapper changes the dish. Parchment puffs high and browns a little at the edges, and it makes the best show at the table. Foil seals tighter and copes with a grill, but it neither puffs nor browns, and long contact with acid such as tomato or lemon can pit it. Banana leaf, softened first over a flame or in hot water so it folds without splitting, adds a faint grassy, tea-like aroma; corn husks, fig leaves and vine leaves each lend their own scent. A crust of salt or of dough works on the same idea, sealing a whole fish or joint as it bakes.

A parcel that leaks lets the steam out, so the fish dries and the paper never puffs: fold tighter and overlap every crimp. Hard vegetables beside soft fish mean the garnish was cut too thick; cut it fine or blanch it first. A pool of thin liquid means too much wine or watery vegetables. Because the parcel hides the fish, the commonest fault is overcooking, so cut fillets to an even thickness and time them.

At Brennan's the Gulf Fish en Papillote wraps the day's Gulf fish in banana leaf instead of paper, with tomato, Castelvetrano olives, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices. The fish changes with the catch, so learn it at lineup. New Orleans knows the method from Antoine's pompano, which has its own entry.

Opening the parcel is the moment. Whether it is opened at the table, and by whom, is a lineup question; when it is, the parcel is cut across and folded back away from the guest, so the steam rises away from faces and the aroma reaches the table first. Warn the guest that the steam is hot. Name the fish, describe the leaf and the garnish, and send any question about the crab or the almonds to the kitchen.

faults.fault: The parcel does not puff and the fish is dry
faults.cause: Loose folds let the steam escape.
faults.fix: Crimp in small, tight, overlapping folds all the way round and twist the tip.

faults.fault: Hard, raw vegetables beside cooked fish
faults.cause: The garnish was cut too thick for the fish's cooking time.
faults.fix: Cut it in fine julienne or blanch it before it goes in.

faults.cause: Fillets of uneven thickness, or timing by guesswork.
faults.fix: Cut even portions, time by thickness and check a test parcel with a probe.

faults.cause: Too much wine or stock, or watery vegetables.
faults.fix: Use 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) of liquid and drain wet vegetables well.

faults.cause: The oven was too hot or the parcel touched the oven walls.
faults.fix: Bake at about 200°C (392°F) on a tray, with room around each parcel.

brennans.how: The day's Gulf fish is wrapped in banana leaf with tomato, Castelvetrano olives, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds, and steams in its own juices. Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest about the steam.

cards.front: What does en papillote mean?
cards.back: In paper: food sealed in a parcel and baked, so it steams in its own juices and keeps its aroma until the parcel is opened.

cards.front: Why does fish en papillote stay moist?
cards.back: The sealed parcel traps the liquid and juices as steam, so the fish cooks gently in its own vapour and nothing escapes.

cards.front: What goes into a classic parcel, in order?
cards.back: Buttered parchment, a bed of finely cut aromatics, the seasoned fish, butter or oil and a splash of wine, then tightly crimped edges.

cards.front: Why must the edges of the parcel be crimped tight?
cards.back: Any gap lets the steam out, so the parcel fails to puff and the fish dries instead of steaming.

cards.front: How do you time a fish en papillote?
cards.back: By thickness: about 12 to 15 minutes at about 200°C (392°F) for a fillet 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick.

cards.front: What does it mean when the parcel puffs?
cards.back: The inside has reached full steam and the fish is cooking hard. It does not prove the fish is done: time by thickness, probe a test parcel, then send it while still puffed.

cards.front: Why are the vegetables in a parcel cut so fine?
cards.back: They must cook in the few minutes the fish takes; thick pieces would stay hard, so they are cut in julienne or blanched first.

cards.front: How is a parcel opened at the table?
cards.back: Cut across and folded back away from the guest, so the hot steam rises away and the aroma reaches the table first.

cards.front: What do parchment, foil and banana leaf each bring?
cards.back: Parchment puffs and browns for show; foil seals tight but stays flat; banana leaf adds a faint grassy, tea-like aroma.

cards.front: Where does the sauce of an en papillote come from?
cards.back: From the parcel itself: the wine, the butter and the fish's own juices gather as it steams and are served with it.

cards.front: How does Brennan's make its en papillote?
cards.back: The Gulf Fish en Papillote wraps the day's Gulf fish in banana leaf with tomato, Castelvetrano olives, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds.

questions.q: What does the French en papillote mean?
questions.answer: In paper
distractors: In butter
In the oven
In a pot
questions.why: The papillote is the paper parcel: the food is sealed inside and baked, steaming in its own juices with its aromatics.

questions.q: A parcel comes out flat and the fish is dry. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The folds let the steam escape
distractors: The oven was too cool to brown it
The fish was seasoned too early
The parcel held too little butter
questions.why: A sealed parcel traps steam and puffs; loose crimps let the steam out, so the fish bakes dry instead of steaming.

questions.q: How is the cooking time for fish en papillote judged?
questions.answer: By the thickness of the fillet
distractors: By the weight of the whole parcel
By the colour of the paper
By the amount of wine added
questions.why: Steam cooks from the outside in, so thickness sets the time: about 12 to 15 minutes for a fillet 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick.

questions.q: Why are carrots and leeks cut in fine julienne for a parcel?
questions.answer: So they cook as fast as the fish
distractors: So they brown against the paper
So they soak up all the wine
So the parcel folds flatter
questions.why: The parcel cooks for minutes only; thick vegetables would stay hard while the fish finished, so they are cut fine or blanched first.

questions.q: When a parcel is opened at the table, how is it done?
questions.answer: Cut it and fold it back away from the guest
distractors: Tear it open towards the guest
Lift the whole parcel off the plate by one corner
Pierce it once and leave it closed
questions.why: The steam inside is hot; folding the paper back away from the guest sends it up and away while the aroma reaches the table.

questions.q: What does a banana leaf add that parchment does not?
questions.answer: A faint grassy, tea-like aroma
distractors: A crisp, browned crust on the fish
A sharp, smoky char
A salty, briny seasoning
questions.why: Banana leaf holds the moisture just as paper does, and its own scent passes faintly to the fish as it steams.

questions.q: What wraps the Gulf Fish en Papillote at Brennan's?
questions.answer: Banana leaf
distractors: Baking parchment
Aluminium foil
A salt crust
questions.why: Brennan's wraps the day's Gulf fish in banana leaf instead of paper, with tomato, Castelvetrano olives, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds.

questions.q: What does a puffed parcel tell the cook?
questions.answer: The inside has reached full steam
distractors: The paper is about to scorch and burn
The wine has all evaporated
The fish needs turning over
questions.why: Steam building inside lifts the paper; the fish is cooking hard, but the time and a probe, not the puff, say when it is done.

entries.title: Confit
entries.summary: From the French confire, to preserve: meat salted, then cooked slowly submerged in fat until it is meltingly tender, and kept under that fat. Duck leg is the classic; garlic, tomato and fish are cooked the same gentle way in oil.
entries.guest: Our duck leg is confit, kohn-FEE: cured with salt, then cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, and crisped before it comes to you so the skin crackles.

paras: Confit, said kohn-FEE, comes from the French confire, to preserve. It is the larder method of Gascony and the south-west of France, from the days before refrigeration: duck or goose legs salted, cooked slowly while submerged in their own fat, then stored in crocks sealed under that fat for months. The salt draws out moisture and seasons the meat; the fat shuts out air.

What began as preserving became a reason in itself. Cooked gently below the simmer, the tough, sinewy leg turns meltingly tender as its connective tissue softens, yet it stays moist, because the fat around it holds the heat steady and lets no water boil away. The meat does not turn greasy: little of the fat enters it. In French pastry the same word means candied, fruit cooked slowly in sugar syrup, as in fruits confits.

Duck leg confit starts with a cure. Rub the legs with about 30 g of salt for each 1 kg (2.2 lb) of duck, about 3 per cent of their weight, with crushed garlic, thyme, bay and black pepper, and leave them covered in the fridge overnight, 8 to 24 hours. Rinse off the salt and dry the legs well; left too long in the cure, the meat turns hard and over-salted.

Lay the legs snugly in a pan, cover them completely with melted duck fat, and cook them in a low oven or over the lowest flame, the fat barely moving, with only a few small bubbles rising from the meat, about 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F). After about 2.5 to 3 hours, sometimes more, a skewer slides into the thigh with no resistance and the meat begins to pull from the bone. Hotter fat fries the meat into stringy toughness instead.

To keep it, let the legs cool in the fat, pressed down so every piece is covered, and chill them; the fat seals out air. The dark jelly that settles beneath is the meat's own juice: good in a sauce, but it spoils sooner than fat, so for a long keep it is lifted away. To serve, lift a leg from the fat, wipe it and crisp it skin side down in a pan over medium heat, or in a hot oven, until the skin shatters, handling it gently, because the meat is now fragile.

Confit reaches well beyond duck. Goose, pork and duck gizzards, gésiers, are cured and cooked the same way in south-western France. Garlic cloves cooked slowly in oil until soft and sweet are garlic confit; tomatoes baked slowly in olive oil with garlic and herbs are tomato confit; fish such as salmon or tuna can be cooked very gently in oil until just set. Onion confit, cooked down slowly with sugar and vinegar, borrows the sugar sense of the word.

A confit in oil does not keep the way a cured duck leg under fat once did. Garlic or vegetables held in oil at room temperature can grow the botulism toxin, so garlic and tomato confit are kept chilled and used within days, under the kitchen's own dating rules. In a modern kitchen duck confit lives in the fridge too.

At Brennan's the Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit, crisped and served on a cornbread and chive waffle. Rohan is a special Mallard and Pekin cross raised for D'Artagnan in New York State, not a breed. Menus often describe confit as cooked in its own fat, though kitchens use pooled duck fat, so describe the method in general and promise no house cure or cooking times.

Say confit plainly: duck leg cured, cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, then crisped, so the skin crackles and the meat falls from the bone. Guests often expect it to be greasy; it is not, because the meat cooks in the fat without soaking it up. Questions about the waffle and what goes into it go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Salt cure
ratios.value: About 30 g for each 1 kg (2.2 lb) of duck legs, about 3 per cent

ratios.label: Cure time
ratios.value: 8 to 24 hours, covered, in the fridge

faults.cause: The fat was too hot, frying the meat instead of cooking it gently.
faults.fix: Keep the fat barely moving, about 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F).

faults.cause: Too much salt, or too long in the cure.
faults.fix: Weigh the salt at about 3 per cent, cure for 8 to 24 hours and rinse well.

faults.cause: Too short a cure, or too little salt.
faults.fix: Cure overnight with the measured salt and aromatics.

faults.cause: Not crisped before serving, or crowded into a cool pan.
faults.fix: Crisp skin side down over medium heat or in a hot oven until it shatters.

faults.cause: The meat was not fully covered, or its juices were left under the fat.
faults.fix: Cover every piece with strained fat, lift away the jelly for a long keep, and chill.

cards.front: What does confit mean?
cards.back: From the French confire, to preserve: meat salted, cooked slowly submerged in fat until tender, and kept under that fat.

cards.front: How is a duck leg cured for confit?
cards.back: Rubbed with about 30 g of salt for each 1 kg (2.2 lb), with garlic, thyme and bay, and left overnight: the salt seasons the meat and draws out moisture. Then it is rinsed and dried.

cards.front: How hot is the fat for a duck confit?
cards.back: Barely moving, about 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F): hot enough to soften the sinew, gentle enough not to fry the meat.

cards.front: How do you know a confit leg is cooked?
cards.back: After about 2.5 to 3 hours a skewer slides into the thigh with no resistance and the meat starts to pull from the bone.

cards.front: Why does a tough leg turn tender in confit?
cards.back: Long, gentle heat softens its connective tissue, while the surrounding fat holds the heat steady and lets no moisture boil away.

cards.front: Is confit greasy, given that it cooks in fat?
cards.back: No: the meat cooks in the fat but takes up little of it, so it is moist and rich rather than oily, especially once the skin is crisped.

cards.front: How is duck confit kept?
cards.back: Cooled and chilled with every piece covered in fat, which shuts out air; the meat jelly beneath is lifted away for a long keep.

cards.front: How is a confit leg finished for service?
cards.back: Lifted from the fat, wiped, then crisped skin side down in a pan or a hot oven until the skin shatters, and handled gently.

cards.front: Name three confits beyond duck.
cards.back: Garlic cloves cooked slowly in oil, tomatoes baked slowly in olive oil, and fish such as salmon cooked very gently in oil.

cards.front: Why are garlic and tomato confits kept chilled?
cards.back: Garlic or vegetables in oil at room temperature can grow the botulism toxin, so they are chilled and used within days.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish carries a confit?
cards.back: The Duck Confit Waffle: a Rohan duck leg made as confit and crisped, on a cornbread and chive waffle.

cards.front: What is a Rohan duck?
cards.back: A special Mallard and Pekin cross raised for D'Artagnan in New York State; call it a cross, never a breed.

questions.q: The French verb confire, behind the word confit, means what?
questions.answer: To preserve
distractors: To roast
To smoke
To braise
questions.why: Confit began as a way to keep meat through the winter: salted, cooked slowly in fat and sealed under it.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature should the fat sit for a duck confit?
questions.why: Fat that is barely moving softens the leg's connective tissue slowly; frying temperatures would toughen the meat, and lukewarm fat would barely cook it.

questions.q: What does the overnight salt cure do for a duck confit?
questions.answer: Seasons the meat and draws out moisture
distractors: Melts the fat under the skin
Turns the skin crisp and brown in the oven
Makes the duck fat clearer
questions.why: Salt seasons the leg through and pulls out moisture, the old basis of preserving; too much or too long makes it hard and salty.

questions.q: How does a cook tell that a confit leg is ready?
questions.answer: A skewer slides into the thigh easily
distractors: The fat starts to boil hard
The skin turns dark brown
The leg floats up to the surface of the fat
questions.why: After about 2.5 to 3 hours in fat that is barely moving, the meat yields to a skewer with no resistance and begins to leave the bone.

questions.q: A guest worries that confit will be greasy. What is true?
questions.answer: The meat takes up little of the fat
distractors: It is soaked in fat to the bone
It is drained and fried again in oil
It is cooked in water, not fat
questions.why: The fat surrounds and gently cooks the meat without soaking into it, so a crisped confit leg is rich and moist rather than oily.

questions.q: How is a confit duck leg finished before it goes out?
questions.answer: Crisped skin side down until it shatters
distractors: Boiled briefly in stock to warm it right through
Served cold straight from the fat
Grilled hard over a high flame
questions.why: Crisping in a pan or a hot oven turns the soft skin crackling, while the fragile, tender meat warms through underneath.

questions.q: Why must garlic confit in oil be kept chilled?
questions.answer: Garlic held in oil at room temperature can grow botulism toxin
distractors: Chilling makes the garlic sweeter
Warm oil slowly turns the garlic green and bitter
Cold oil keeps the cloves crisp
questions.why: Garlic or vegetables sealed in oil at room temperature give botulism a place to grow, so oil confits are chilled and used within days.

questions.q: At Brennan's, which duck is made as confit for the Duck Confit Waffle?
questions.answer: A Rohan duck leg
distractors: A Pekin duck breast
A wild mallard breast
A Muscovy duck leg
questions.why: The waffle carries a Rohan duck leg, D'Artagnan's Mallard and Pekin cross, made as confit and crisped; the duck breast is roasted for the tasting menu.
